claim: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) serves diverse biological functions in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, including neurotransmission in vertebrates.
source: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) serves diverse biological functions in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, including neurotransmission in vertebrates.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge about GABA's functions.

claim: Human and murine myeloid mononuclear phagocytes possess a conserved and tightly regulated GABAergic machinery with expression of GABA metabolic enzymes and transporters, GABA-A receptors and regulators, and voltage-dependent calcium channels.
source: Here, a comprehensive characterization of human and murine myeloid mononuclear phagocytes revealed the presence of a conserved and tightly regulated GABAergic machinery with expression of GABA metabolic enzymes and transporters, GABA-A receptors and regulators, and voltage-dependent calcium channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including qPCR, immunocytochemistry, and functional assays.

claim: Infection challenge with Toxoplasma gondii and Neospora caninum activated GABAergic signaling in phagocytes.
source: Infection challenge with the common coccidian parasites Toxoplasma gondii and Neospora caninum activated GABAergic signaling in phagocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased GABA secretion and altered gene expression upon parasite challenge.

claim: GABAergic signaling in parasitized phagocytes is linked to calcium responses and migratory activation.
source: Using gene silencing and pharmacological modulators in vitro and in vivo in mice, we identify the functional determinants of GABAergic signaling in parasitized phagocytes and demonstrate a link to calcium responses and migratory activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging, motility assays, and pharmacological inhibition studies.

claim: GABAergic signaling plays a regulatory role in the host-pathogen interplay between phagocytes and invasive coccidian parasites.
source: The findings reveal a regulatory role for a GABAergic signaling machinery in the host-pathogen interplay between phagocytes and invasive coccidian parasites.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro and in vivo experimental data showing effects on parasite dissemination.

claim: The co-option of GABA underlies colonization of the host by a Trojan horse mechanism.
source: The co-option of GABA underlies colonization of the host by a Trojan horse mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that parasites hijack phagocyte migration for dissemination.

claim: One third of the global human population is estimated to be chronically infected by T. gondii.
source: One third of the global human population is estimated to be chronically infected by T. gondii (Pappas et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: T. gondii and N. caninum exploit the inherent migratory ability of DCs and monocytes for dissemination via a Trojan horse mechanism.
source: Paradoxically, T. gondii and N. caninum exploit the inherent migratory ability of DCs and monocytes for dissemination via a Trojan horse mechanism (Sangaré et al., 2019; Lambert et al., 2006; Lambert et al., 2009; Courret et al., 2006; Collantes-Fernandez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Within minutes of active invasion by T. gondii, DCs adopt a hypermigratory phenotype that mediates rapid systemic dissemination in mice.
source: Within minutes of active invasion by T. gondii, DCs adopt a hypermigratory phenotype that mediates rapid systemic dissemination in mice (Kanatani et al., 2017; Weidner and Barragan, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GABAergic inhibition of DCs hampers dissemination of T. gondii.
source: GABAergic inhibition of DCs hampers dissemination of T. gondii (Kanatani et al., 2017; Fuks et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Upon invasion by tachyzoites, a rapid increase of migrated distances and elevated velocities were recorded in infected murine bone marrow-derived DCs (mBMDCs), compared with unchallenged cells.
source: Upon invasion by tachyzoites (Figure 1A), a rapid increase of migrated distances (Figure 1B) and elevated velocities (Figure 1C) were recorded in infected murine bone marrow-derived DCs (mBMDCs), compared with unchallenged cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C including microscopy and motility tracking.

claim: Human monocytes, monocyte-derived DCs (hMoDCs) and primary myeloid DCs (hMDCs) freshly isolated from blood of human donors consistently exhibited hypermotility upon challenge with T. gondii.
source: Similarly, human monocytes, monocyte-derived DCs (hMoDCs) and primary myeloid DCs (hMDCs) freshly isolated from blood of human donors consistently exhibited hypermotility upon challenge (Figure 1D,E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F and supplementary figures.

claim: Phagocytes expressed transcripts of enzymes for GABA synthesis and catabolism.
source: Further, phagocytes expressed transcripts of enzymes for GABA synthesis and catabolism (Figure 1G)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: GABA synthesis and catabolism enzymes were up- and downregulated, respectively, upon challenge with T. gondii.
source: which were up- and downregulated, respectively, upon challenge with T. gondii (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Elevations of GABA concentrations in the supernatants were detected shortly after challenge and increased over time.
source: Consistent with this, elevations of GABA concentrations in the supernatants were detected shortly after challenge and increased over time (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Challenge of mononuclear phagocytes with separate strains of T. gondii and N. caninum resulted in elevated concentrations of GABA in cell supernatants.
source: Further, challenge of mononuclear phagocytes with separate strains of the two coccidia resulted in elevated concentrations of GABA in cell supernatants (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: mBMDCs consistently expressed mRNAs for 10 out of the 19 GABA-A R subunits (α3, α4, α5, β2, β3, γ1, γ2, δ, ρ1, ρ2).
source: Interestingly, mBMDCs consistently expressed mRNAs for 10 out of the 19 GABA-A R subunits (α3, α4, α5, β2, β3, γ1, γ2, δ, ρ1, ρ2) (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Expression of GABA-A R subunits was conserved in a murine DC line (JAWSII).
source: and expression of GABA-A R subunits was conserved in a murine DC line (JAWSII) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: hMoDCs from healthy donors consistently expressed the α4, ρ1, ρ2 and ρ3 subunits, while expression of the α3, β1 and β3 subunits was only detected in some donors.
source: Further, hMoDCs from healthy donors consistently expressed the α4, ρ1, ρ2 and ρ3 subunits, while expression of the α3, β1 and β3 subunits was only detected in some donors (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Freshly isolated hMDCs from human donors consistently expressed β2, θ, ρ1 and ρ2 subunits of GABA-A Rs.
source: Finally, freshly isolated hMDCs from human donors consistently expressed β2, θ, ρ1 and ρ2 subunits of GABA-A Rs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Challenge with T. gondii modulated the subunit mRNA expression in murine and human DCs.
source: Interestingly, challenge with T. gondii modulated the subunit mRNA expression in murine and human DCs (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C, D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Transcriptional expression of the α6, β2 and θ subunits, undetectable in unchallenged hMoDCs, was consistently observed in challenged hMoDCs.
source: Of note, transcriptional expression of the α6, β2 and θ subunits, undetectable in unchallenged hMoDCs, was consistently observed in challenged hMoDCs (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Immunocytochemical analyses yielded signal consistent with expression of α3, α5, β3 and ρ1 subunits.
source: Immunocytochemical analyses with available antibodies yielded signal consistent with expression of α3, α5, β3 and ρ1 subunits (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A broad range GABA-A R open-channel blocker (picrotoxin) and α, β and ρ subunit selective inhibitors (L655 708, SCS and TPMPA, respectively), efficiently inhibited T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in mBMDCs.
source: A broad range GABA-A R open-channel blocker (picrotoxin) and α, β and ρ subunit selective inhibitors (L655 708, SCS and TPMPA, respectively), efficiently inhibited T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in mBMDCs (Figure 3A,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 3A, C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: GABA-A R inhibitors efficiently inhibited T. gondii-induced hypermotility in hMoDCs.
source: A broad range GABA-A R open-channel blocker (picrotoxin) and α, β and ρ subunit selective inhibitors (L655 708, SCS and TPMPA, respectively), efficiently inhibited T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in mBMDCs (Figure 3A,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), hMoDCs (Figure 3B,D)
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: GABA-A R inhibitors efficiently inhibited T. gondii-induced hypermotility in freshly isolated hMDCs and monocytes.
source: A broad range GABA-A R open-channel blocker (picrotoxin) and α, β and ρ subunit selective inhibitors (L655 708, SCS and TPMPA, respectively), efficiently inhibited T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in mBMDCs (Figure 3A,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), hMoDCs (Figure 3B,D) and, freshly isolated hMDCs and monocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Blockade of GABA transporters (SNAP) inhibited hypermotility in parasitized mBMDCs.
source: Further, we took advantage of the finding that blockade of GABA transporters (SNAP) inhibited hypermotility in parasitized mBMDCs (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Blockade of GABA transporters reduced GABA concentrations in the supernatants.
source: Further, we took advantage of the finding that blockade of GABA transporters (SNAP) inhibited hypermotility in parasitized mBMDCs (Figure 3E,F) with reduced GABA concentrations in the supernatants (Figure 5F)
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Hypermotility was rescued by an allosteric modulator of β2/β3-containing GABA-A Rs (etomidate), but not by an allosteric modulator of δ subunit-containing GABA-A Rs (allopregnanolone).
source: Importantly, hypermotility was rescued by an allosteric modulator of β2/β3-containing GABA-A Rs (etomidate), but not by an allosteric modulator of δ subunit-containing GABA-A Rs (allopregnanolone) (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The shRNA probes significantly silenced target transcription in mBMDCs.
source: Second, the shRNA probes were validated in neuronal cell lines known to express GABA-A Rs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E) and significantly silenced target transcription in mBMDCs (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4A and validation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: The shRNA probes significantly silenced target transcription in hMoDCs.
source: Second, the shRNA probes were validated in neuronal cell lines known to express GABA-A Rs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E) and significantly silenced target transcription in mBMDCs (Figure 4A) and hMoDCs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B and validation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: Hypermotility was abolished in shβ3- and shρ1-treated mBMDCs.
source: In contrast, hypermotility was abolished in shβ3- and shρ1-treated mBMDCs (Figure 4C,D,G), demonstrating the implication of β3 and ρ1 subunits.
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 4C, D, and G.

claim: In shα3-treated cells, hypermotility was significantly reduced, albeit not abolished, indicating a contribution by the α3 subunit.
source: In shα3-treated cells (with two separate constructs), hypermotility was significantly reduced, albeit not abolished, indicating a contribution by the α3 subunit.
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 4C, D, and G.

claim: In hMoDCs, hypermotility was significantly reduced in shα4-treated cells, but not in shρ2-treated cells, indicating primarily a dependence on the α4 subunit for hypermotility.
source: In hMoDCs, hypermotility was significantly reduced in shα4-treated cells, but not in shρ2-treated cells (Figure 4E,F,G), indicating primarily a dependence on the α4 subunit for hypermotility.
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 4E, F, and G.

claim: hMoDCs and mBMDCs expressed GABA transporters.
source: In addition to GABA synthesis enzymes (Figure 1G), hMoDCs and mBMDCs expressed GABA transporters (Figure 5A, C)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: GABA transporter expression was modulated by challenge with T. gondii.
source: In addition to GABA synthesis enzymes (Figure 1G), hMoDCs and mBMDCs expressed GABA transporters (Figure 5A, C), whose expression was modulated by challenge with T. gondii (Figure 5B, D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B and D.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of GABA synthesis (SC) inhibited hypermotility and reduced GABA concentrations in the supernatants of hMoDCs.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of GABA synthesis (SC) (Figure 5E, H) or transportation (SNAP) (Figure 5E, G) inhibited hypermotility and reduced GABA concentrations (Figure 5F) in the supernatants of hMoDCs
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 5E, H and ELISA data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of GABA transportation (SNAP) inhibited hypermotility and reduced GABA concentrations in the supernatants of hMoDCs.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of GABA synthesis (SC) (Figure 5E, H) or transportation (SNAP) (Figure 5E, G) inhibited hypermotility and reduced GABA concentrations (Figure 5F) in the supernatants of hMoDCs
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 5E, G and ELISA data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Exogenous GABA and GABA-A R agonism (muscimol) fully reconstituted hypermotility in hMoDCs in presence of GABA synthesis inhibitor.
source: Further, exogenous GABA and GABA-A R agonism (muscimol) fully reconstituted hypermotility in hMoDCs in presence of GABA synthesis inhibitor (Figure 5E, H).
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 5E and H.

claim: The amounts of secreted GABA in the supernatant were strongly reduced in GAD67-silenced infected hMoDCs.
source: Importantly, the amounts of secreted GABA in the supernatant were strongly reduced in GAD67-silenced infected hMoDCs, approached amounts secreted by unchallenged cells and contrasted with maintained GABA secretion by mock- or shLuc-transduced infected cells (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: GAD67-silenced infected hMoDCs exhibited abrogated hypermotility.
source: Finally, GAD67-silenced infected hMoDCs exhibited abrogated hypermotility (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: mBMDCs transcriptionally express NKCCs and KCCs.
source: A transcriptional expression screen (Supplementary file 1) detected mRNAs of NKCCs and KCCs in mBMDCs (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: hMoDCs transcriptionally express NKCCs and KCCs.
source: A transcriptional expression screen (Supplementary file 1) detected mRNAs of NKCCs and KCCs in mBMDCs (Figure 6A) and in hMoDCs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Upon T. gondii challenge, a strong upregulation of NKCC1 was observed in mBMDCs.
source: Notably, upon T. gondii challenge, a strong upregulation of NKCC1 was observed in mBMDCs, which was less accentuated in hMoDCs (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Immunolabeling and western blotting indicated presence of NKCC1/2 proteins in mBMDCs.
source: Immunolabeling and western blotting indicated presence of NKCC1/2 proteins in mBMDCs (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry and western blot data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Antagonism with bumetanide resulted in impaired T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in mBMDCs.
source: Interestingly, antagonism with bumetanide, at concentrations known to inhibit NKCC but not KCC activity in neurons (Orlov et al., 2015), resulted in impaired T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in mBMDCs (Figure 6G,I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 6G, I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Antagonism with bumetanide resulted in impaired T. gondii-induced hypermotility in hMoDCs.
source: Interestingly, antagonism with bumetanide, at concentrations known to inhibit NKCC but not KCC activity in neurons (Orlov et al., 2015), resulted in impaired T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in mBMDCs (Figure 6G,I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), hMoDCs (Figure 6H,J)
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 6H and J.

claim: Antagonism with bumetanide resulted in impaired T. gondii-induced hypermotility in hMDCs and monocytes.
source: Interestingly, antagonism with bumetanide, at concentrations known to inhibit NKCC but not KCC activity in neurons (Orlov et al., 2015), resulted in impaired T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in mBMDCs (Figure 6G,I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), hMoDCs (Figure 6H,J), hMDCs and monocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Hypermotility was abolished in NKCC1-silenced mBMDCs and hMoDCs.
source: Importantly, hypermotility was abolished in NKCC1-silenced mBMDCs and hMoDCs (Figure 6M,N).
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 6M and N.

claim: Stimulation with GABA or with the GABA-A R agonist muscimol failed to reconstitute hypermotility of mBMDCs in the presence of the NKCC1 antagonist bumetanide.
source: First, we observed that stimulation with GABA or with the GABA-A R agonist muscimol failed to reconstitute hypermotility of mBMDCs in the presence of the NKCC1 antagonist bumetanide (Figure 6O)
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 6O.

claim: Upon silencing of GABA synthesis (shGAD67), addition of exogenous GABA reconstituted hypermotility.
source: Upon silencing of GABA synthesis (shGAD67), addition of exogenous GABA reconstituted hypermotility. In contrast, in NKCC1-silenced cells, GABA failed to reconstitute hypermotility (Figure 6P,Q, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 6P, Q and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In NKCC1-silenced cells, GABA failed to reconstitute hypermotility.
source: Upon silencing of GABA synthesis (shGAD67), addition of exogenous GABA reconstituted hypermotility. In contrast, in NKCC1-silenced cells, GABA failed to reconstitute hypermotility (Figure 6P,Q, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 6P, Q and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: hMoDCs expressed mRNA of 9 out of 10 known VDCC subtypes, with highest relative expression of CaV1.3, 1.4 and 3.1.
source: First, we detected mRNA expression of 9 out of 10 known VDCC subtypes in hMoDCs, with highest relative expression of CaV1.3, 1.4 and 3.1 (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A and Supplementary files 1 and 2.

claim: Challenge with T. gondii led to a prominent upregulation of CaV1.3, 2.2 and 2.3 mRNAs.
source: Moreover, challenge with T. gondii led to a prominent upregulation of CaV1.3, 2.2 and 2.3 mRNAs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: VDCC inhibition abolished T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in hMoDCs.
source: Importantly, VDCC inhibition abolished T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in hMoDCs (Figure 7C,D)
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: VDCC inhibition abolished T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in hMDCs, monocytes and mBMDCs.
source: Importantly, VDCC inhibition abolished T. gondii-/N. caninum-induced hypermotility in hMoDCs (Figure 7C,D), hMDCs, monocytes and mBMDCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, C.

claim: A structural analogue of nifedipine with positive ionotropic effect (Bay K8644) reconstituted hypermotility of infected hMoDCs in the presence of GABA synthesis inhibitor (SC).
source: Moreover, a structural analogue of nifedipine with positive ionotropic effect (Bay K8644) reconstituted hypermotility of infected hMoDCs in the presence of GABA synthesis inhibitor (SC) (Figure 7E)
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Bay K8644 significantly enhanced motility in unchallenged hMoDCs.
source: Moreover, a structural analogue of nifedipine with positive ionotropic effect (Bay K8644) reconstituted hypermotility of infected hMoDCs in the presence of GABA synthesis inhibitor (SC) (Figure 7E) and also significantly enhanced motility in unchallenged hMoDCs (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Silencing of CaV1.3 yielded abolished hypermotility.
source: The prominent effect of CaV1.3 inhibition prompted us to silence CaV1.3 expression (Figure 7F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,D, Supplementary file 3), which yielded abolished hypermotility (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: This is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 7G and H, and gene silencing data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Perfusion of exogenous GABA consistently generated transient cytosolic Ca2+ elevations.
source: Importantly, perfusion of exogenous GABA consistently generated transient cytosolic Ca2+ elevations, which were antagonized by the GABA-A R blocker picrotoxin (broad inhibitor) and with maintained responsiveness by purinergic Ca2+ channels to ATP (Figure 8B,C,D; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8B, C, D and Video 1.

claim: GABA-induced Ca2+ elevations were antagonized by the GABA-A R blocker picrotoxin.
source: Importantly, perfusion of exogenous GABA consistently generated transient cytosolic Ca2+ elevations, which were antagonized by the GABA-A R blocker picrotoxin (broad inhibitor) and with maintained responsiveness by purinergic Ca2+ channels to ATP (Figure 8B,C,D; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8B, C, D and Video 1.

claim: Transients generated by L-type VDCC agonism (Bay K) were effectively antagonized by CaV1.3 inhibition (CPCPT), indicative of a prominent role for CaV1.3 in the measured Ca2+ responses.
source: Further, transients generated by L-type VDCC agonism (Bay K) were effectively antagonized by CaV1.3 inhibition (CPCPT), indicative of a prominent role for CaV1.3 in the measured Ca2+ responses (Figure 8E,F,G, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8E, F, G and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: T. gondii-infected cells responded to GABA with transient Ca2+ influx.
source: Finally, T. gondii-infected cells responded to GABA with transient Ca2+ influx. In individual cell recordings, Ca2+ influx was significantly reduced or abolished by application of inhibitors of β-subunit containing GABA-A Rs (SCS) and by picrotoxin, with maintained responses to ATP (Figure 8H,I,J).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8H, I, and J.

claim: In T. gondii-infected cells, Ca2+ influx in response to GABA was significantly reduced or abolished by application of inhibitors of β-subunit containing GABA-A Rs (SCS) and by picrotoxin.
source: Finally, T. gondii-infected cells responded to GABA with transient Ca2+ influx. In individual cell recordings, Ca2+ influx was significantly reduced or abolished by application of inhibitors of β-subunit containing GABA-A Rs (SCS) and by picrotoxin, with maintained responses to ATP (Figure 8H,I,J).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8H, I, and J.

claim: The ratio of pretreated vs non-treated parasitized mBMDCs was significantly lower in spleen for both GABA-A R inhibitor and NKCC1 inhibitor treatments compared with that for non-treated condition.
source: Importantly, the ratio of pretreated vs non-treated parasitized mBMDCs was significantly lower in spleen for both GABA-A R inhibitor and NKCC1 inhibitor treatments compared with that for non-treated condition (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Non-significant differences in the ratio of pretreated vs non-treated parasitized mBMDCs were observed in peritoneum.
source: In contrast, non-significant differences were observed in peritoneum (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Compared with the non-treated condition, pharmacological treatments significantly decreased the parasite loads in spleen and liver.
source: Importantly, compared with the non-treated condition, treatments significantly decreased the parasite loads in spleen and liver (Figure 9E, Figure 9—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: This is supported by plaquing assay and qPCR data shown in Figure 9E and Figure 9—figure supplement 2D, E.

claim: When gene-silenced mBMDCs challenged with T. gondii were adoptively transferred into mice, significantly reduced parasite loads were quantified in peripheral organs.
source: Finally, we silenced the GABA-A R subunit ρ1 or NKCC1, two GABA signaling targets with a significant impact on mBMDC migration in vitro (Figure 4, Figure 6). When gene-silenced mBMDCs challenged with T. gondii were adoptively transferred into mice, significantly reduced parasite loads were quantified in peripheral organs (Figure 9F)
evidence: This is supported by plaquing assay data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of GABA-A Rs or NKCC1 yielded a significant reduction of parasites loads in the brain by day seven post-inoculation.
source: Moreover, pharmacological inhibition of GABA-A Rs or NKCC1 yielded a significant reduction of parasites loads in the brain by day seven post-inoculation (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is supported by plaquing assay data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: GABA is synthesized cytosolically and secreted in vesicle-independent fashion, likely by transport through GATs, for tonic modulations of GABA-A Rs in immune cells, similar to neurons.
source: This supports the notion that GABA is synthesized cytosolically and secreted in vesicle-independent fashion, likely by transport through GATs, for tonic modulations of GABA-A Rs in immune cells, similar to neurons (Kaufman et al., 1991; Feldblum et al., 1993).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data on GABA synthesis and secretion, supported by citations to neuronal literature.

claim: The different phagocyte types consistently expressed a repertoire of GABA-A R subunits sufficient to constitute functional channels, that is: at least one α, one β and one third type of subunit, or homopentamer-forming ρ subunits.
source: Yet, the different phagocyte types consistently expressed a repertoire of GABA-A R subunits sufficient to constitute functional channels, that is: at least one α, one β and one third type of subunit, or homopentamer-forming ρ subunits.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data showing expression of multiple GABA-A R subunits.

claim: Silencing of the α4 subunit (but not ρ2) or β3 and ρ1 subunits (but not α3) abolished hypermigration of human and murine DCs, respectively.
source: Importantly, silencing of the α4 subunit (but not ρ2) or β3 and ρ1 subunits (but not α3) abolished hypermigration of human and murine DCs, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by gene silencing and motility assay data.

claim: NKCC1 plays a crucial role in the regulation of GABA signaling in phagocytes.
source: By pharmacological inhibition and gene silencing in vitro and in vivo, we show that NKCC1 plays a crucial role in the regulation of GABA signaling in phagocytes.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological and gene silencing experiments in vitro and in vivo.

claim: Silencing of the VDCC subtype CaV1.3 in human DCs abrogated T. gondii-induced hypermotility.
source: Moreover, silencing of the VDCC subtype CaV1.3 in human DCs abrogated T. gondii-induced hypermotility, in line with our observations in murine DCs (Kanatani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by gene silencing and motility assay data, and by citation to previous work.

claim: CaV1.3 is determinant to the motogenic action of GABA-A R activation.
source: Jointly, this demonstrates that CaV1.3 is determinant to the motogenic action of GABA-A R activation.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing CaV1.3's role in calcium signaling and hypermotility.

claim: T. gondii and N. caninum induce GABAergic signaling in parasitized phagocytes.
source: Our data establish that T. gondii and N. caninum, two coccidian parasites with a broad range of vertebrate hosts, induce GABAergic signaling in parasitized phagocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing GABA secretion and gene expression changes upon parasite challenge.

claim: Hijacking a conserved GABAergic system offers the advantage of inducing migratory activation of shuttle phagocytes within minutes after active invasion to favor systemic dissemination in vertebrate hosts.
source: From a perspective of intracellular parasitism, hijacking a conserved GABAergic system offers the advantage of inducing migratory activation of shuttle phagocytes within minutes after active invasion (Weidner et al., 2013) to favor systemic dissemination in vertebrate hosts (Lambert et al., 2006; Courret et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DCs initiated GABA secretion shortly after T. gondii invasion.
source: Consequently, DCs initiated GABA secretion shortly after T. gondii invasion.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data showing GABA secretion at early time points.

claim: The rapid onset and tight regulation of GABAergic signaling by-passes the need for, presumably slower, transcriptional regulation.
source: Thus, the rapid onset and tight regulation of GABAergic signaling by-passes the need for, presumably slower, transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of rapid GABA secretion and functional responses.

claim: The GABA signaling regulator NKCC1 plays an important role in the hypermigration of parasitized phagocytes, presumably by impacting chloride concentration and thus, GABA-A R function.
